claims.text: The target alloy is bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Sintering routes for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr produce oxygen-bearing, imperfect microstructures.
The modeled sintered material contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen together with typical grain boundaries and associated imperfections.
A multiscale model can couple ab initio electronic and phonon calculations with Monte Carlo or Boltzmann defect-transport simulations.
Measurements exist for a sintered bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing about 1 wt.% oxygen in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Quantum effects and reduced phonon populations are critical in the 0–200 K regime.
Phonon anharmonicity and defect scattering dominate thermal transport in the 300–1200 K regime.
Oxygen interstitials, grain boundaries, and local strain fields alter electron and phonon scattering rates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Changes in electron and phonon scattering rates modify the alloy's overall thermal conductivity.
Representing oxygen and defect-induced scattering redistributes phonon and electron transport channels relative to an ideal crystal.
Oxygen and defect scattering reduce thermal conductivity relative to perfect-lattice predictions.
At low temperatures, defect scattering compensates for low phonon populations.
At high temperatures, enhanced anharmonicity and oxygen-driven scattering reduce thermal transport.
The defect-inclusive model will predict thermal conductivity within approximately ±10% throughout both specified temperature regimes.
Existing perfect-crystal analytical models have thermal-conductivity errors of approximately ±20–30% or more for the relevant material.
Existing analytical models are restricted to perfect, defect-free crystals and give inaccurate estimates for defect-bearing sintered HfNbTaTiZr.
The model is applicable to bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr made by sintering routes that produce a defect structure similar to the approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimen.
The model may not extend to highly purified single crystals or processing routes that suppress defect formation.
Grain-size distributions and possible secondary phases may affect thermal conductivity in addition to oxygen.
Failure to improve accuracy by at least 10%, errors remaining above ±20%, or failure to significantly outperform the perfect-crystal model would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires errors within ±10%, but the falsification rule explicitly rejects the model only when errors remain above ±20% or it fails to significantly outperform the baseline. A 15% error could violate the predicted outcome without clearly satisfying the stated falsification condition.

An accuracy improvement of at least 10% is treated as equivalent to keeping errors below ±20%, but these are not mathematically equivalent without a specified baseline error and a definition of whether improvement is absolute or relative.
